conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us see how mood, anxiety, and energy levels have been for you over the past seven days. Your answers stay completely confidential between you and the care team, and this is a judgment-free space—there’s no right or wrong response, only what’s true for you. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally, and we’ll go at whatever pace feels comfortable.

Let’s start gently:  
Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt harder to do lately?

[pauses, looking down at her hands in her lap]

I… yeah, it’s been harder. My sister sent me a silly video the other night and I sort of half-smiled, but it felt like work. Everything feels heavier, you know? Like I remember I used to laugh a lot—my husband and I would joke around all the time—but lately even when something’s objectively funny, I’m just… flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

Not really… I mean, I can tell when something’s supposed to be funny, but it’s like the laugh gets stuck. Mostly I just feel tired and kind of numb.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake—but now it feels like, “what’s the point?” I still do them sometimes, but it’s more going through the motions. I keep hoping the spark will come back, but this week it just… hasn’t.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes mist over, fingers twisting the edge of her sweater]

All the time. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap unless I held her, and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—other moms get their babies on schedules.” When she fusses I immediately wonder what I missed, what I did to mess her up already. I know logically babies cry, but my brain keeps whispering it’s my fault for not being good enough at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[sighs, rubbing her palms on her knees]

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not gaining enough weight, or I’ll lie awake picturing her bassinet catching fire. Nothing sets it off, really—it just shows up and sits on my chest until I’ve triple-checked the monitor or Googled another “is this normal?” article. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[draws a slow, shaky breath]

A few times this week. It hits out of nowhere—like yesterday morning she was napping in the bassinet and suddenly I felt this wave of terror, my chest tight and my hands clammy. I kept thinking, “What if she stops breathing right now?” It was so strong I had to get up and check on her, even though she was fine. Once I saw her little chest moving, I could breathe again, but the feeling hung around for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods, eyes filling]

Yes… most days I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, she wants to cluster-feed, the laundry’s everywhere, and I can’t seem to catch my breath. I’ll start one task and get pulled into another, and by evening I’ve finished nothing and still feel bone-tired. I keep telling myself, “It’s just one day at a time,” but even that feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[swallows hard]

Yeah… I’ll finally get her down around ten, but then I’m lying there staring at the ceiling, thoughts racing—did I wash the bottles, is she breathing, what if tomorrow’s just as hard? I drop off for maybe an hour, then every tiny grunt over the monitor jolts me awake. By three a.m. I’m still tossing and turning, stomach in knots. I’m exhausted, but sleep just won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

[Voice drops, eyes stay on the blanket folded in her lap]

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I see the sunshine outside, but it doesn’t feel warm. I’ll be holding her close and still feel this ache in my chest that won’t lift. Sometimes I just sit on the couch and cry because everything feels heavy and colorless.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, pressing a tissue under her eyes]

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. The other night I finally got her to sleep, and instead of feeling relieved I just started sobbing—quiet so I wouldn’t wake her. It felt like all the sadness I’d been pushing down just spilled out. I couldn’t even name one exact reason; it was everything and nothing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks up quickly, shaking her head]

No—no, never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and low, but hurting myself has never crossed my mind. My baby needs me, and even on the hardest days that’s the one thing that feels clear.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: laughter and excitement are distant memories, replaced by a persistent gray cloud of sadness, <sym>self-doubt</sym>, and <sym>exhaustion</sym>. Daily tasks feel unmanageable, <sym>sleep</sym> is elusive despite extreme tiredness, and waves of <sym>anxiety</sym> or even <sym>panic</sym> arrive without warning. Yet you remain firmly devoted to your baby, and the idea of self-harm has never entered your mind-an important strength we'll build upon.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient indicates complete inability to laugh despite recognizing humor, describing emotional numbness and fatigue</sym>, <sym>Patient reports minimal to no enjoyment or anticipation, describing activities as pointless and merely going through the motions, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports self-blame "all the time," with specific examples of feeling at fault for baby's fussing and napping issues, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, unprovoked anxiety episodes that are exhausting and persistent, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed most days, unable to manage basic tasks, and exhausted, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with persistent ache and inability to feel joy, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple tearful episodes, including a recent bout of unexplained crying, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med> (≥5 symptoms daily for 2 wks). You endorsed: (1) depressed mood "pretty much every day", (2) loss of interest "feels like what's the point", (3) guilt/self-blame "all the time", (4) fatigue, (5) concentration difficulty, (6) sleep disruption beyond infant care, (7) recurrent tearfulness. Anxiety items (Q4, Q5) indicate <med>postpartum anxiety</med> overlap. Score ≥14 mandates urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. No self-harm ideation (Q10) lowers immediate safety risk but does not negate need for prompt treatment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent evaluation with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> this week; request formal diagnostic assessment for <med>postpartum depression/anxiety</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments: individual <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, sertraline or compatible antidepressant, and mother-baby support groups
3. Plan daily 30-min rest window; accept help with chores to protect limited energy and support recovery
4. Share results with a trusted partner/friend who can accompany you to appointments and monitor changes
5. Keep crisis numbers saved: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your local 24-h mental-health urgent line-even though self-harm is not on your mind, rapid access is wise
6. Re-screen using EPDS in 2 weeks to track intervention response; arrange immediate re-contact if worsening mood, hopelessness, or any self-harm thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**  
*Date:* [today’s date] – 10-item EPDS-style interview  

**Presenting symptoms endorsed:**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Pathologic guilt/self-blame regarding parenting competence (Q3)  
- Unexplained, intrusive anxiety and panic episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Sleep disturbance solely related to mood preoccupation (Q7)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed / inability to cope with daily tasks (Q6)  
- Diminished capacity for pleasure or humor (Q1)  

**Observed patterns:**  
- Symptoms present “pretty much every day this week”  
- Functional impact: tasks unfinished, exhaustion, social withdrawal  
- Absence of self-harm ideation; protective factor = infant needs her (Q10)  

**Screening significance:**  
- High endorsement of depressive items consistent with probable postpartum depression; co-occurring anxiety/panic symptoms suggest probable postpartum anxiety.  
- Total estimated EPDS score ≥ 12 (individual item scoring not completed).  

**Safety/risk factors:**  
- No suicidal or self-harm thoughts reported. – **Safety concern: none at present.**  
- Reassure and continue monitoring; if any emergent self-harm ideation → immediate escalation protocol.  

**Plan:**  
- Discuss findings; offer referral to OB/GYN or behavioral health for formal evaluation and evidence-based treatment consideration (therapy, medication consult, support group).  
- Provide crisis / emergency contact numbers.
